Because the sense organ and the object meet, olfactory consciousness arises;
subsequently, mental consciousness arises and forcibly grasps the characteristics of fragrance.
Due to this, all dharmas—such as afflictions, good, and evil—come into being; therefore, it is called "smelling fragrance."
Turning back to observe the mind that perceives fragrance, one does not perceive its form or appearance.
One should know that the perception of fragrance and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent; this is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Fourth, regarding the practitioner who cultivates *śamatha* when the tongue experiences flavors:
as each flavor is experienced, they know it to be like obtaining a taste within a dream or an illusion.
If they encounter a delicious flavor that accords with their desires, they do not give rise to attachment.
When encountering unpleasant tastes that go against one's desires, one does not give rise to a mind of anger;
when encountering tastes that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable, one does not give rise to conceptual thoughts or discriminations—this is called the cultivation of *śamatha*.
What is meant by the cultivation of *vipaśyanā* at the time the tongue experiences taste?
One should form this thought:
"The flavor currently being experienced is truly unobtainable. Why is this so?
The six flavors, both internal and external, are by nature without discrimination.
Due to the conjunction with the internal faculty of the tongue, gustatory consciousness arises.
Subsequently, mental consciousness arises and forcibly grasps the characteristics of the flavor.
"Therefore, there exist all dharmas, such as afflictions, good, and evil.
When one turns back to observe the consciousness that perceives flavors, no characteristics are seen.
One should know that the experiencer of flavors and all dharmas are ultimately empty and quiescent; this is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Fifth, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* when the body experiences contact:
whatever contact is perceived, one immediately knows it to be like a shadow, a magical illusion, and unreal.
If one experiences a pleasant contact that accords with the mind, one does not give rise to craving or attachment.
If one experiences painful contact that is contrary to one's feelings, one does not give rise to anger or affliction;
if one experiences contact that is neither contrary nor favorable, one does not give rise to recollections or conceptual discriminations—this is called the cultivation of śamatha.
How does one practice contemplation when the body experiences contact?
One should form this thought:
"Qualities such as lightness and heaviness, cold and heat, roughness and smoothness are called 'contact' (spraṣṭavya)."
The six parts, beginning with the head, are called the body.
The nature of touch is illusory, and the body is likewise unreal;
through the conjunction of causes and conditions, body-consciousness arises.
Next, mental consciousness arises, which recollects, imagines, and discriminates the characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and so forth; therefore, it is called "contact-feeling" (*vedanā-sparśa*).
When one turns back to observe the mind that conditions contact, no form or characteristic is seen.
One should know that the experiencer of contact and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent; this is called the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā).

Sixth, regarding the characteristics of cultivating serenity (śamatha) and insight within the consciousness of mind cognizing mental objects, this has already been explained in detail above in the section on initial sitting.

From this point upward, the characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are cultivated based on the six sense faculties; they are applied according to their intended function, each embodying the meaning of the five preceding stages. These have already been analyzed in detail herein, so they will not be further expounded now.

If a practitioner can cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā in all situations—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—one should know that this person is truly cultivating the Mahāyāna path.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha told Subhūti:

'If, when a bodhisattva walks, he knows he is walking; when he sits, he knows he is sitting; and so on, up to wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, blinking with a single-minded focus, and entering and emerging from meditative concentration—then one should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva Mahāyāna.'"
"Furthermore, if a person can practice the Mahāyāna in this way amidst all circumstances, that person is the most excellent, the most supreme, and peerless in the world."
The verse in the *Śāstra* says:
"Sitting leisurely amidst the forest trees, Tranquil, extinguishing all evils,
Serene and attaining single-mindedness— This joy is not the joy of the heavens."
When people seek worldly gain—fame, fine robes, and comfortable bedding—such pleasures are not secure;
in their pursuit of profit, they know no satiety.
But one who wears a patched robe in a secluded place, with mind ever unified in every movement and stillness, finds true peace.
Relying on the clarity of one’s own wisdom, one contemplates the true nature of all phenomena;
among all the various dharmas, one enters them all through equal contemplation.
With understanding-wisdom and a tranquil mind, one is peerless within the three realms.

7. The Arising of Wholesome Roots: Regarding the seventh practitioner who is able to thus skillfully cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the contemplation that enters emptiness from the conventional, their body and mind will become luminous and pure while sitting; at that time, various kinds of wholesome roots will arise, which one must recognize and understand.
Now, to briefly clarify the manifestations of the arising of roots of goodness, there are two different types:
first, the manifestation of external roots of goodness.
This is as follows:

The cultivation of roots of goodness such as giving, observing the precepts, being filial toward one's parents and elders, making offerings to the Triple Gem, and engaging in various studies and learning—these are external matters;
if they are not part of correct cultivation, they may be confused with the realms of Māra, and thus will not be distinguished here.
II. The Characteristics of the Arising of Internal Roots of Goodness.

Regarding the threefold intention for the development of the roots of goodness within the dharma-gates of various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the first clarifies the characteristics of the arising of these roots of goodness.
There are five kinds of distinctions:
first, the signs of the arising of the roots of goodness on the path of tranquility.
Because the practitioner skillfully cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, body and mind become harmonious and supple, and deluded thoughts come to rest.

Because of this, one becomes self-aware of the mind and gradually enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*), giving rise to concentrations such as those of the desire realm and the threshold stage (*anāgamya*). Body and mind become utterly still and empty, and the concentrated mind is peaceful and secure.
Within this samādhi, one perceives no characteristics whatsoever of body or mind.
Thereafter, whether after one sitting, two sittings, or even for one day, two days, a month, or two months, if one does not exert oneself in cultivation, there will be no regression and no loss.

While in meditative concentration, one suddenly becomes aware of the movement of body and mind, giving rise to the eight tactile sensations; these are what are known as the sensations of bodily pain, itching, cold, warmth, lightness, heaviness, roughness, and smoothness.

When it is triggered, the body and mind become tranquil, subtle, joyful, blissful, and pure beyond compare; this is the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness of fundamental dhyāna within the path of mindfulness of breathing.

When a practitioner, while in the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm, suddenly perceives the length of the inhalation and exhalation and observes that all the pores of the body have become entirely porous and open, they immediately see the thirty-six internal constituents within the body with the mind’s eye, just as one sees hemp or beans when opening a granary. Their heart is filled with great joy and surprise, becoming tranquil, peaceful, and blissful; this is the sign of the arising of the special roots of goodness (*viśeṣa-mūla*) associated with following the breath.
2. The signs of the arising of the roots of goodness of the contemplation of impurity.

If a practitioner, while in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm, experiences within this meditative absorption a state where body and mind are empty and still, and suddenly sees the corpses of others—male or female—after death, becoming bloated, putrefying, and oozing with worms and pus;

seeing their white bones strewn about, his mind feels a mixture of sorrow and joy, and he develops a sense of weary revulsion toward what he once cherished. This is the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness of the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*).

Or, while in a state of meditative concentration, one may suddenly perceive the impurity of the internal body and the bloated, disarrayed state of external bodies; seeing one's own skeleton from head to foot with the joints interlocking, and having seen this, the mind becomes settled and secure, awakening to impermanence, developing revulsion for the five desires, and ceasing attachment to self and person—this is the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness of the *prātikūlyavimokṣa* (reversal of attachment).

Alternatively, within a state of meditative concentration, one may perceive that both the internal body and the external body, as well as all flying birds and running beasts, clothing and food, houses, mountains, and forests, are entirely impure; this is the sign of the arising of the root of goodness of great impurity.
Third, the signs of the arising of the roots of goodness of a compassionate mind.

Because the practitioner cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, if they attain the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) of the desire realm, within this concentration they suddenly give rise to a mind of compassion, mindful of sentient beings; or, by taking as an object the appearance of a loved one obtaining happiness, they immediately enter a profound concentration, wherein their inner mind is joyful and pure beyond compare.
It is the same for neutral persons, enemies, and even all sentient beings throughout the ten directions in the five realms of existence.

Upon arising from meditative concentration, their mind is joyful and pleasant; toward whomever they look, their countenance is always harmonious. This is the sign of the manifestation of the roots of goodness of the mind of loving-kindness.
The manifestations of the arising of the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) may be understood by analogy with this.
Fourth, the manifestation of the arising of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) through the contemplation of causes and conditions (*idampratyayatā-pratītyasamutpāda*):

Because the practitioner cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, they attain the "not-yet-reached" stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) of the desire realm. Their body and mind become tranquil and concentrated, and a sudden awakening arises. As they investigate the various causes and conditions—such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—throughout the three periods of time, they do not perceive a person or a self (*ātman*). Thus, they depart from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism, shatter all views of grasping, and attain stable composure. As their liberating wisdom unfolds, the mind gives rise to the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*), and they no longer dwell upon worldly matters. This applies even to the analytical discernment within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). This is the manifestation of the arising of the roots of goodness through the contemplation of causes and conditions.
Five: The Signs of the Arising of the Roots of Goodness through Mindfulness of the Buddha.

Because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they attain the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the desire realm, their body and mind become empty and tranquil. Suddenly, they recollect the inconceivable marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddhas' merits; the inconceivable dharmas such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the samādhis, and the liberations; the inconceivable supernormal transformations, unimpeded preaching of the Dharma, and the vast benefiting of sentient beings;
and all such immeasurable merits that are inconceivable.

When one gives rise to such thoughts, a heart of love and reverence immediately arises; samādhi is manifested, and body and mind experience bliss, purity, and tranquility, free from all unwholesome signs. Upon arising from meditative concentration, the body becomes light and agile, and one personally realizes that one’s merit is sublime and majestic, becoming beloved and respected by others. This is the sign of the manifestation of the roots of goodness of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).

Furthermore, because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they attain clarity and purity of body and mind, they may give rise to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, the loathsomeness of the world, the impurity of food, and the notions of death, separation, and exhaustion; or they may give rise to mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, precepts, renunciation, and the devas; or mindfulness of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); or the various perfections (*pāramitā*) such as the six transcendences, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transformations, and so forth—the signs of the arising of all such dharma-gates should be extensively analyzed therein.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"If one restrains the mind to a single point, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Second, regarding the discernment of the true and the false, there are two parts:

First, distinguishing the signs of the arousal of false and counterfeit dhyāna. When a practitioner arouses any of the aforementioned dhyānas, according to the dharma aroused by its respective cause, there may be:

physical agitation; at times, the body feels heavy as if weighed down by objects; at times, the body feels light as if about to fly; at times, it feels as if bound; at times, it feels limp and drooping; at times, one suffers from a chilling cold; at times, one suffers from intense heat; at times, one perceives various extraordinary realms; at times, the mind becomes darkened and obscured; at times, various evil thoughts arise; at times, the mind dwells on external distractions and miscellaneous worldly matters; at times, there is joyous restlessness; at times, there is sorrowful lamentation; at times, one experiences unpleasant tactile sensations such that the hair on the body stands on end; or at times, there is great bliss accompanied by a state of stupor and intoxication.
When various such false dharmas arise together with meditative concentration, they are termed "false and deceptive."
If a person becomes attached to this false concentration, they will correspond with the ninety-five kinds of ghost-spirit dharmas; they will frequently lose their minds and fall into madness.

At times, when various ghosts and spirits perceive that a person is fixated on their methods, they will exert their power to induce false concentrations and false wisdom, as well as eloquence and supernatural powers, thereby deluding and agitating worldly people.

Those of foolish and ignorant views claim to have attained the fruits of the Path; they cause all to believe and submit, yet their inner minds are inverted, and they exclusively practice demonic arts to delude and confuse the world.
When such a person’s life ends, they will never encounter a Buddha again and will fall back into the realm of ghosts and spirits.
If they frequently practice evil dharmas while sitting, they will immediately fall into hell.
When a practitioner cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, if they realize such meditative states as these and encounter these various false and deceptive signs, they should immediately eliminate them.
How does one eliminate them?
If one knows it to be false and deceptive, and with a correct mind neither accepts nor clings to it, it shall immediately subside and vanish.
One should employ right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) to destroy it, and it shall then be extinguished.
Second, distinguishing the signs of the arising of true and correct dhyāna.

When the practitioner gives rise to various dhyānas while seated, there are no such false dharmas as those described above. As each dhyāna arises, they immediately perceive it to be in accord with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): empty, luminous, and pure; the inner mind is joyful;
there is serene bliss without any obscuration;
the wholesome mind unfolds, and faith and reverence increase.
His wisdom and discernment were clear and distinct, and his body and mind were supple;
he was subtle, wondrous, empty, and tranquil, feeling weary of and distressed by the mundane world;
being unconditioned and free from desire, he moved with sovereign ease.
This is the sign of the manifestation of right dhyāna.
It is like working with an evil person, where one is constantly troubled by their provocations;
yet, if one works with a virtuous person, one perceives their excellence over time.
The discernment of the signs of the arising of the two kinds of meditation—false and correct—is likewise so.
Third, clarifying the application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to nurture all roots of goodness:
when various roots of goodness arise during seated practice, one should employ the two methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to cultivate them so that they progress.
If it is appropriate to employ calming (*śamatha*), then cultivate it through calming;
if it is appropriate to employ insight (*vipaśyanā*), then cultivate it through insight.
This is as previously explained, providing a brief indication of the general meaning.

8. Awareness of the Deeds of Māra. Regarding the eighth [section], "Awareness of the Deeds of Māra": *Māra* in the language of India is called "The Killer" (*Śatru*) in the language of Qin. He robs the practitioner of the wealth of merit and kills the life-force of wisdom; for this reason, he is named "Evil."

Regarding the works of Māra: while the Buddha takes as his task the deliverance of sentient beings through merit and wisdom so that they enter nirvāṇa, Māra constantly takes as his task the destruction of the roots of goodness in sentient beings, causing them to wander in saṃsāra.
If one can settle the mind in the Right Path, then it is precisely because the Path is exalted that one realizes the intensity of Māra’s activity.
One must still skillfully recognize the works of Māra, of which there are four kinds:

first, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*); second, the Māra of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu-māra*); third, the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*); and fourth, the Māra of spirits and deities (*deva-piśāca-māra*).
These three types are all common worldly matters that arise in accordance with one's own mind; they must be correctly eliminated by one's own mind, and thus will not be analyzed here.
Regarding the signs of ghosts, spirits, and māras, these matters must be known; I shall now briefly explain them.
There are three kinds of ghosts, spirits, and māras:
first, the *jingmei* (malevolent sprites).

The animals of the twelve hours manifest through transformations in various forms and colors; they may take the shape of young maidens or elderly elders, and even assume terrifying bodies and other diverse forms, thereby vexing and deluding practitioners.
These various malevolent spirits (*piśācīs*) seek to harass the practitioner and each arrives at its respective hour; one must skillfully recognize them.
If they arrive during the hour of the Tiger (*yínshí*), they are certainly beasts such as tigers;
if they arrive during the hour of the Rabbit (*mǎoshí*), they are certainly animals such as rabbits and deer.
If they come during the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), they must be dragons, turtles, and the like;
if they come during the hour of the Snake (9–11 a.m.), they must be snakes, pythons, and the like;
if they come during the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–1 p.m.), they must be horses, donkeys, camels, and the like.
If they come during the hour of Wei (15:00–17:00), they must be sheep and the like;
if they come during the hour of Shen (17:00–19:00), they must be monkeys and the like;
if they come during the hour of You (19:00–21:00), they must be chickens, crows, and the like.
If it comes during the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.), it must be a dog, a wolf, or the like;
if it comes during the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), it must be a pig or the like;
if it comes during the hour of Zi (11 p.m.–1 a.m.), it must be a rat or the like.
If it arrives during the hour of the Ox (the second watch), it must be a cow or similar creature.
If the practitioner observes that it habitually arrives at this time, he should recognize it as a beast-spirit, call out its name, and rebuke it; it will then immediately apologize and vanish.
Second are the *tūṇḍika* ghosts.

They also inflict various kinds of afflictions and provocations upon the practitioner—such as crawling over the practitioner’s head and face like insects or scorpions, piercing and stinging with a shimmering brilliance;
or striking the practitioner in both armpits.
Some suddenly embrace people;
some speak with clamorous and noisy voices;
and some take the forms of various beasts—manifesting manifold strange appearances—to come and harass travelers.
One should immediately become aware of this, close one's eyes with single-minded focus, and secretly revile them, saying:
"I now recognize you! You are the *sthalagitri*, who eats the foul-smelling incense of fire within Jambudvīpa, a person of wrong views and a delighter in breaking the precepts;
I now uphold the precepts and shall never fear you!"
If they are renunciants, they should recite the *Prātimokṣa*;
if they are laypeople, they should recite the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
The ghosts will then retreat, crawling away on their hands and knees.
Thus, regarding the various manifestations of creating obstacles and distressing others, as well as other methods for their elimination, these are all explained in detail within the *Dhyāna-sūtra*.
Third is the affliction by Māra.
This Māra frequently manifests the appearances of the three kinds of five-sense objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) to destroy the wholesome mind:
first, he creates circumstances that contradict one's desires, namely, the five sense objects that are terrifying and cause people to feel fear.
Second, agreeable objects cause the five desirable sense-objects to engender attachment in the mind.
Third, neutral objects—those that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable—cause the five sense-objects to agitate and distract the practitioner.
For this reason, Māra is called "The Killer";
he is also called "The Flower-Arrowed One," and also "The Five-Arrowed One," because he shoots at the five faculties of human beings.
Within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), various objective spheres (*viṣaya*) are created to delude and confuse practitioners.
Those that create favorable objects may manifest as parents, brothers, images of the Buddhas, or the forms of handsome men and women—objects of affection—that cause people’s minds to become attached.
As for creating objects that contradict one's emotions: they may take the form of tigers, wolves, lions, or rākṣasas, manifesting various terrifying images to frighten the practitioner.

Those who create circumstances that are neither contrary nor favorable are those who cause ordinary matters to disturb the human mind and cause one to lose meditative concentration; therefore, they are called Māras.

Or, they produce various pleasant and unpleasant sounds, various fragrant and foul odors, various pleasant and unpleasant tastes, and various realms of suffering and pleasure to come into contact with the human body—all of these are the deeds of Māra.
Their manifestations are numerous, which I shall not describe in detail here.
To state the essentials:
if various objects of the five senses cause disturbance to people, leading them to lose wholesome dharmas and give rise to all manner of afflictions, these are all the armies of Māra.
Because it can destroy the equal Dharma of the Buddha, it gives rise to various obstructive dharmas that hinder the Path, such as desire, sorrow, anger, and sleep.
As stated in a verse of the sutra:
"Desire is your first army, Sorrow is the second,"
Hunger and thirst are the third army; craving is the fourth;
sleep is the fifth army; fear is the sixth;
doubt and regret are the seventh army; and anger is the eighth.
Gain and offerings, false reputation—these are the nine; self-exaltation and arrogance toward others is the tenth.
Such are the many armies that crush and submerge those who have left the household life.
By the power of my meditative wisdom, I shall destroy all these armies of yours.
"Once I have attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall deliver all people.
Once the practitioner has recognized these demonic activities, they must immediately repel them.
There are two methods for repelling them:
First, one should employ *śamatha* (calm abiding) to repel them.

Whenever one encounters any external demonic realms, one should recognize them all as false and deceptive; thus, one neither grieves nor fears, and neither grasps nor rejects them through deluded conceptualization or discrimination.
When the mind is stilled and silent, those [distractions] will naturally cease.
Second, one should repel them by practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

If you encounter various demonic realms as described above and they do not subside through the practice of calming (*śamatha*), you should instead turn back and contemplate the perceiving mind; since no location for it can be found, what is there to cause affliction?
When you observe in this manner, they will soon vanish and pass away.
If they do not depart quickly, you should simply maintain a correct mind, harbor no thoughts of fear, disregard your own life, and remain unmoved through right mindfulness.

To know that the suchness of the realm of Māra is the very suchness of the realm of the Buddha—since the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are a single suchness without a second suchness—to understand this is to neither abandon the realm of Māra nor grasp at the realm of the Buddha. Thus, the Buddha-dharma will naturally manifest before one, and the realms of Māra will spontaneously vanish.
Furthermore, if you see the realms of Māra and they do not subside, you need not give rise to anxiety;
if you see them subside and vanish, likewise do not give rise to joy. Why is this?

I have never seen anyone practicing meditation who saw a Māra transform into a tiger or a wolf to come and devour them, nor have I ever seen a Māra transform into a man or a woman to come and act as a husband or wife.

When such illusions and transformations occur, the foolish do not understand them; they give rise to fear and attachment in their minds. Because of this, their minds become distracted, they lose their meditative concentration, and they go mad, thereby bringing suffering upon themselves. All of this is the result of the practitioner’s own lack of wisdom leading to their affliction; it is not the doing of Māra.

If various demonic realms disturb and confuse the practitioner, or do not depart even after months or years have passed, one should simply maintain an upright mind and right mindfulness with firm resolve, not begrudging body or life, and harbor no anxiety or fear. One should recite the mantras for subduing demons from the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, chanting them silently.
Keep the Three Jewels in mind.
When emerging from meditative concentration, you should likewise recite mantras for self-protection, practice repentance with a sense of shame and remorse, and recite the Prātimokṣa.
The heterodox does not disturb the orthodox; after a long time, it will extinguish itself.
The deeds of Māra are numerous and cannot be fully described; one must recognize them well.

Therefore, a practitioner at the initial stage of the path must personally attend upon a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), for there are such difficult matters as these: Māra enters the human mind and can cause the practitioner’s spirit and heart to become deranged, leading to either excessive joy or sorrow, which consequently results in affliction and even death.

At times, they may cause others to attain various false meditative concentrations, wisdom, supernormal powers, and dharanis; they preach the Dharma and convert others so that all people believe and submit to them, yet later they destroy people's worldly and supramundane wholesome deeds and ruin the True Dharma.
Such variations are manifold and cannot be fully described.
Here, I shall briefly indicate their essentials so that practitioners, while engaged in seated meditation, do not mistakenly grasp at various mental objects.
To state the essential point:

if one wishes to dispel the heterodox and return to the orthodox, one should contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena and skillfully cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; then there is no heterodoxy that will not be destroyed.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* says:
"Except for the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.
As it is said in a verse:
"If one discriminates and conceptualizes, that is the net of Māra."
"Neither moving nor discriminating—this is the Seal of the Dharma. Chapter Nine:

Healing Illnesses When a practitioner settles the mind to cultivate the Way, they may suffer from illnesses of the four great elements. Due to the current practice of contemplation, the mind and breath strike together, thereby provoking a latent illness.
Alternatively, at times one may fail to properly harmonize the three factors of body, mind, and breath; because of internal or external transgressions, illnesses arise.
Now, regarding the method of seated meditation (*dhyāna*), if one can skillfully apply the mind, then the four hundred and four ailments will naturally be cured;
if the application of the mind is misplaced, then the four hundred and four ailments will arise because of it.

Therefore, whether practicing for oneself or transforming others, one should skillfully identify the source of the ailment and be well-versed in the methods for treating internal maladies while seated in meditation.
Should such a malady be provoked, it will not only create obstacles to the practice of the Path, but may even lead to the loss of one's life.
Now, within the method for treating illness, there are two points:
first, clarifying the manifestations of the illness; second, clarifying the methods for treating the illness.
First, regarding the clarification of the manifestations of the illness:
Although the manifestations of illness follow many paths, they can be summarized as no more than two types:
first, the symptoms of illness arising from the increase or decrease of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If the earth element increases, there will be swellings, knots, heaviness, and emaciation of the body; thus, one hundred and one such ailments arise.

If the water element increases excessively, then phlegm and cold-natured conditions will swell and fill the body; ailments such as indigestion, abdominal pain, and diarrhea—hundreds and even one of these—will arise.

If the fire element increases excessively, then the body will be parched with chills and fever, the limbs and joints will all ache, there will be bad breath, and the passage of stool and urine will be obstructed—hundreds and even one of these ailments will arise.

If the wind element increases excessively, then the body becomes light and suspended, trembling and painful; the lungs feel stifled and constricted, with nausea and labored breathing; thus, one hundred and one such ailments arise.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"If one of the four great elements is disturbed, one hundred and one illnesses arise.
If all four great elements are disturbed, four hundred and four illnesses move simultaneously."
"When the four great elements give rise to illness, each has its own specific signs; one should observe them while sitting in meditation and within dreams.
Second, there are the signs of afflictions arising in the five viscera."
Illnesses arising from the heart manifest as bodily chills and fevers, headaches, dryness of the mouth, and so forth, because the heart governs the mouth.

Illnesses arising from the lungs manifest as distension and fullness of the body, distressing pain in the four limbs, oppression in the chest, nasal congestion, and so forth, because the lungs govern the nose.

For those who suffer from ailments arising from the liver, there is generally an absence of joy; they are sorrowful and unhappy, plagued by grief, anxiety, and anger, and experience headaches, blurred vision, and dizziness, because the liver governs the eyes.

For those suffering from conditions arising from the spleen, there is a wandering wind throughout the body and face, characterized by pricking, itching, and pain, as well as a loss of appetite for flavors; this is because the spleen governs the tongue.

Regarding those who suffer from ailments arising from the kidneys: there will be such symptoms as a sensation of obstruction in the throat, abdominal distension, and deafness, because the kidneys govern the ears.
Although the illnesses arising from the five viscera are numerous and each has its own specific signs, they can be discerned by observing them during sitting meditation and in dreams.
Thus, the illnesses arising from the four great elements and the five viscera have various causes and numerous symptoms that cannot be fully described.
If a practitioner wishes to cultivate the dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, should an ailment arise, they ought to skillfully understand its cause.
These two types of illness are both triggered by internal and external causes.

If one is injured externally by cold, wind, or heat, or if food and drink are not properly digested, and the illness manifests from these two locations, one should know that it is triggered by external factors.

If, due to an unbalanced application of the mind, the practice of contemplation becomes deviant and perverse, or if, at the time of the emergence of meditative factors, one does not know how to adopt or reject them, these two types of affliction arise; this is the manifestation of illness arising from within.
Furthermore, there are three different causes and conditions for contracting illness:
first, contracting illness through the increase or decrease of the four great elements and the five viscera, as previously explained;
second, contracting illness caused by malevolent spirits.
Third, there are illnesses acquired through karmic retribution.
Such illnesses as these, when first contracted, can be treated immediately and are very easily cured.
If they persist for a long time, the illness becomes chronic; the body becomes emaciated and the disease becomes entrenched, making it difficult to cure even with treatment.
Second, regarding the clarification of the methods for treating illness:
once the origins and manifestations of the illness have been thoroughly understood, one should apply the appropriate methods to treat it.
There are many paths to these methods for treating illness; to state the essentials, they do not go beyond the two types of skillful means: *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
What is the characteristic of using *śamatha* (calm abiding) to treat illness?
A certain master says:
"Simply settle the mind in a state of calm abiding upon the site of the illness, and one will be able to cure it."
Why is this so? Because the mind is the master of the retribution for an entire lifetime; it is like a king who, wherever he goes, causes a band of thieves to scatter in all directions.
Next, another teacher said:
"One inch below the navel is called Udāna, which in this context is translated as Dantian (the Cinnabar Field).
If one can settle the mind here and maintain it without distraction for a long duration, many ailments will be cured."
A certain teacher said:

"Constantly keep the mind focused on the soles of the feet; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, do not inquire into these states, and you will be able to cure the illness. Why is this?..."
Because people’s four great elements (mahābhūta) are out of harmony, they suffer from many ailments.
This arises because the mind-consciousness (citta-vijñāna) takes objects above [in the realm of form and formlessness]; thus, it causes the four great elements to become unbalanced.
If one settles the mind in the lower [realm], the four great elements will naturally become harmonious and well-adjusted, and all illnesses will be eliminated.
A certain teacher said:
"If one simply knows that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, does not grasp at the signs of illness, and dwells in tranquil stillness, there will be much that is cured."
Why is this so? It is because the four great elements are stirred and activated by the mind’s recollections and imaginings, and thus illness arises.
When the mind is stilled and harmoniously joyful, all illnesses are immediately cured.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"What is the root of illness? It is that which is called 'clinging to conditions' (ālambana)."
"How does one sever objective conditions?
It means that the mind finds nothing to be apprehended.
Such various explanations demonstrate that the methods for using cessation (*śamatha*) to treat afflictions are not limited to a single form.
Thus, one knows that the skillful cultivation of the method of *śamatha* can cure all ailments.
Next, to clarify the treatment of illness through *vipaśyanā*,
a master says:
"Regarding the practice of curing illness by means of visualizing the mind and employing the six types of breath: this visualization itself is what cures the illness.
What are these six types of breath?
First, *chui*; second, *hu*; third, *xi*; fourth, *he*; fifth, *xu*; sixth, *xi*."

These six types of breath-regulation are all performed within the lips and mouth through the skillful application of mental visualization; they are executed by turning and shifting the breath, applied with subtle and gentle force.
The verse says:
"The heart belongs to *ha*, the kidneys to *chi*; The spleen to *hu* and the lungs to *xi*—the sages know this well."
"When heat accumulates in the liver organ, the syllable *xu* arrives; when the triple burner (*tridoṣa*) is congested, one simply utters *xi*. A master said:
"If one can skillfully employ visualization and practice the twelve types of breath, one can cure all manner of ailments."

1. Upward breath; 2. downward breath; 3. filling breath; 4. burning breath; 5. increasing breath; 6. decaying breath; 7. warm breath; 8. cold breath; 9. surging breath; 10. sustaining breath; 11. harmonizing breath; 12. replenishing breath.
These twelve breaths all arise from the mind of contemplative visualization.
Now, the characteristics of their respective remedies are briefly explained: the upward breath remedies heaviness;

the downward breath remedies a sense of suspension; the full breath remedies emaciation; the parching breath remedies swelling and distension; the increasing breath remedies wasting and decline; the destructive breath remedies excessive growth; the warm breath remedies cold; the cool breath remedies heat; the surging breath remedies congestion and obstruction; the sustaining breath remedies trembling; the harmonizing breath universally remedies the disharmony of the four great elements; and the replenishing breath provides support for the decay of the four great elements.
"If one skillfully employs this breath, it can universally treat all ailments; this can be understood by inference.
Another teacher said:
"One who skillfully employs the visualization of mental imagery can cure all diseases."
It is like a person suffering from a cold who, by imagining that the fire-element arises within their body, is immediately able to cure the cold.
This is explained in detail among the seventy-two secret methods for treating illness in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
A certain master said:

"Simply employ *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to examine and analyze the four great elements within the body; when the disease of the body cannot be found and the disease of the mind cannot be found, all ailments will naturally subside."
Through such various explanations as these, one employs contemplation to treat illnesses; since the applications differ, if one skillfully grasps their underlying intent, all illnesses can be cured.
One should know that regarding the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā, if a person skillfully grasps their intent, there is no illness that cannot be treated.
However, people of the present age have shallow and dull faculties; when they perform this visualization, it is mostly not accomplished, and thus it has not been transmitted in the world.
Furthermore, one must not additionally study breath-control techniques (*prāṇāyāma*) or fasting (*anaśana*) at this stage, for fear that heterodox views may arise.
Medicines derived from metal, stone, grass, and wood that correspond to the specific ailment may also be taken as an oral remedy.
If it is a disease caused by spirits, one should employ strengthening of the mind along with incantations to assist in the treatment.
If it is a disease resulting from karmic retribution, one must cultivate merit and perform repentance for the affliction to be extinguished.

Regarding these two methods of treating illness, if a practitioner can skillfully attain single-mindedness, they may apply them both to themselves and others, let alone if they possess complete mastery and penetration.

If one knows nothing at all, then illness will arise without remedy; this not only results in the abandonment of the cultivation of the True Dharma, but also poses a threat to one's very life. How, then, could such a person instruct others?
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must thoroughly understand the methods for treating the illnesses of the internal mind;
these methods are not of a single kind, and their mastery depends on the individual—how could they possibly be transmitted through mere words?
Furthermore, when using the mind to treat illness while seated in meditation, one must additionally possess ten dharmas; there will be nothing that does not prove beneficial.

These ten dharmas are: first, faith; second, application; third, diligence; fourth, constant abiding within the conditions; fifth, discerning the methods for the causes of illness; sixth, skillful means; seventh, long-term practice; eighth, knowing what to adopt and what to discard; ninth, maintaining and protecting; tenth, recognizing hindrances.
What is faith? It means having faith that this dharma will certainly be able to cure the illness.
What is its function?
This refers to its regular use according to the occasion.
What is diligence?
It means employing it with focused intensity and without ceasing, until the desired result is achieved as the measure of completion.
What is meant by abiding within conditions?
It refers to the subtle mind that, moment by moment, relies upon the dharmas without shifting its object.
What is meant by the arising of distinct causes and conditions?
As stated above,
what constitutes the skillful means?
It refers to the exhalation and inhalation of breath, the movement of the mind, and the cultivation of mental objects, accomplished with such dexterity that their proper application is never lost.
What is meant by "practicing for a long time"?
It means that even if its benefits are not immediately apparent, one does not count the days or months, but constantly practices without ceasing.
What is meant by "knowing what to adopt and what to discard"?
This means that one recognizes what is beneficial and applies diligence toward it, and recognizes what is detrimental and abandons it, thereby subtly transforming and regulating the mind.
What is meant by "maintaining and guarding"?
It refers to being skillfully aware of the contact with and transgression against various conditions.
What constitutes the obstacles?
It means that when one has gained benefit, one does not speak of it to others; and when one has not suffered loss, one does not give rise to doubt or slander.
If one relies upon these ten dharmas, that which is to be remedied will certainly be effective and not in vain.

10. Realizing the Fruit, the Tenth. When a practitioner thus cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, they are able to understand that all dharmas arise from the mind; because their causes and conditions are false and unreal, they are empty. Because they know emptiness, they do not apprehend the names or characteristics of any dharmas; this is the "stopping that realizes the truth" (tattva-śamatha).

At that time, one does not perceive above a Buddha-fruit to be sought, nor does one perceive below sentient beings to be delivered; this is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, also called the contemplation of the two truths, also called the wisdom-eye, and also called all-knowledge.
If one dwells in this contemplation, one will fall into the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The assembly of śrāvakas and others exclaimed to themselves:"
"If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching and transforming sentient beings, our hearts would find no joy therein.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without arising and without cessation, neither great nor small, and without outflows or conditioned activity."
"Reflecting in this way, one does not give rise to joy.

One should know that if someone sees the unconditioned and enters the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), that person will ultimately never be able to resolve their mind toward supreme enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
This is because their concentration is predominant, and thus they do not see the Buddha-nature.

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings and to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, should not cling to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and enter self-extinction, at that time they should cultivate the contemplation that enters the conventional from emptiness (śūnyatā-prajñapti-praveśa-vipaśyanā).

One should then contemplate with clarity that although the nature of the mind is empty, at the time of encountering conditions, it is also capable of giving rise to all phenomena; just as illusory transformations lack any fixed reality, they nonetheless possess various distinct characteristics such as seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.

When the practitioner contemplates in this manner, although they know that all dharmas are ultimately empty and quiescent, they are able to cultivate various practices within emptiness, like planting trees in the air.
Furthermore, because they can discern the infinite faculties, dispositions, and natures of sentient beings, they preach the Dharma in infinite ways;
and if they can achieve unimpeded eloquence, they are then able to benefit the sentient beings of the six realms.
This is called "stopping according with conditions through skillful means.
It is the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness; it is also called the Contemplation of Equality, the Dharma-eye, and the Knowledge of the Modes of the Path.
Abiding within this contemplation, because the power of wisdom is still slight, although one perceives the Buddha-nature, it is not clearly manifest.
Although a bodhisattva may accomplish these two kinds of contemplation, they are called the "gate of expedient contemplation" and are not the "correct contemplation."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The first two contemplations constitute the path of skillful means.

By means of these two contemplations of emptiness, one attains entry into the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way, wherein one simultaneously illuminates the two truths; with each thought-moment entering quiescence, one naturally flows into the ocean of sarvajñā."

"If a bodhisattva wishes to fully realize all Buddha-dharmas within a single thought-moment, they should cultivate the cessation that stills the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes and practice the correct contemplation of the Middle Way."
What is the cultivation of correct contemplation?
If one realizes that the nature of the mind is neither real nor false, and brings to rest the mind that discriminates between the real and the false, this is called "correct.

To contemplate the nature of the mind as being neither empty nor false, yet without destroying the phenomena of emptiness and the conventional, and if one can thus illuminate and understand it, then one will penetrate the Middle Way regarding the nature of the mind and perfectly illumine the two truths.

If one can perceive the Middle Way and the two truths within one's own mind, then one perceives the Middle Way and the two truths within all phenomena; yet one does not even grasp at the Middle Way and the two truths, because a determinate nature cannot be found.
This is called the Middle Way of Right Contemplation.
As it is said in a verse of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare them to be emptiness."
"It is also called 'provisional designation,' and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

Probing deeply into the intent of this verse, it not only fully elucidates the characteristics of the Middle Way through analytical discernment, but also concurrently clarifies the essential purport of the two preceding types of skillful means for contemplation.
You should know that the middle way of right contemplation is the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of all modes.
If one abides in this contemplation, the powers of concentration and wisdom will be equal, and one will clearly perceive the Buddha-nature.
Abiding securely in the Mahāyāna, their gait is level and upright, swift as the wind; they naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Practicing the conduct of a Tathāgata, entering the chamber of a Tathāgata, donning the robe of a Tathāgata, and sitting upon the seat of a Tathāgata, they adorn themselves with the adornments of a Tathāgata. They attain the purity of the six sense faculties and enter the realm of the Buddha.

To be unstained by and unattached to all phenomena, to have all Buddha-dharmas manifest before one, to achieve the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, and to dwell securely in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*—this is the *sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*.
They enter universally into the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings.

They adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions, uphold the Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas, fulfill all the *pāramitās* of practice, and awaken to and enter the stage of great Bodhisattvas, thereby becoming the equal companions of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
While abiding within the eternally present *dharmatā-kāya*, they are praised and receive predictions of enlightenment by all Buddhas.

They thus adorn the Tuṣita heaven, manifesting the descent of their spirit into a mother’s womb, renouncing the world, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, subduing the hosts of Māra, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of the Dharma, and entering *nirvāṇa*.

One who brings all Buddha-works to ultimate completion throughout the lands of the ten directions and is fully endowed with both the true body (*dharmakāya*) and the responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one attains perfect awakening; one thoroughly realizes the true nature of all phenomena, and this body of wisdom is not realized through another.
It is also said:
"A Bodhisattva who has first generated the mind attains the Tathāgata’s single body as infinite bodies."
It is also said:
"The bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment is himself a Buddha.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Subhūti!..."

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], immediately sit at the site of awakening and turn the wheel of the true Dharma; you should know that such bodhisattvas are as if they were Buddhas.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says:
"The pearl offered by the dragon girl serves as proof.

Scriptures such as these all clarify that the initial resolve is fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas; this is the "A-character gate" (*akāra-mukha*) in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the means for enabling sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the reason for abiding in Great Nirvāṇa through the realization of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Having briefly explained the characteristics of the initial-mind bodhisattva’s realization of the fruit through the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, we shall next clarify the characteristics of the subsequent-mind realization of the fruit.
The realm realized by the subsequent mind is unknowable;
however, as we now infer from what is clarified in the teachings, it ultimately does not depart from the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Why is this so? As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "Diligently extol the wisdom of all Buddhas. Since wisdom is the contemplation of meaning, this explains the fruit by way of contemplation.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the hundredfold liberation is extensively analyzed to explain Great Nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa is the meaning of "cessation" (*śamatha*); this clarifies the fruit by way of cessation. Therefore, it is said that "Great Parinirvāṇa is called the Samādhi of Eternal Quiescence," and "samādhi" is precisely the meaning of cessation.

Although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains the fruit in terms of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it thereby subsumes it within tranquility (*śamatha*); thus it says: "Even unto ultimate nirvāṇa, the mark of eternal quiescence ultimately reverts to emptiness."
Although within *nirvāṇa* the fruit is explained primarily by way of *śamatha*, it nonetheless encompasses *vipaśyanā*; therefore, the three virtues constitute Great *Nirvāṇa*.

Although these two great sūtras differ in the appearance or omission of specific terminology, they both elucidate the ultimate state by means of the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and both clarify the supreme fruit based on the two dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The practitioner should know that the fruits of the beginning, middle, and end are all inconceivable; thus, the newly translated *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata of the past limit is inconceivable; the Tathāgata of the middle limit is adorned with various ornaments; the Tathāgata of the future limit is eternally indestructible."
This is because all [teachings] distinguish their fruits based on the two mental states of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
As a verse in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* says:
"The Buddhas attain liberation from the mind; / The mind, being pure, is called stainless."
"Pure and stainless in the five realms, not receiving [the taints of] form—those who train in this shall accomplish the Great Way.
Regarding the practice of one's vows, one must eliminate the three obstructions and the five hindrances.
If these [afflictions] are not eliminated, then even though one exerts diligent effort, it will ultimately be of no benefit.

This concludes the Essential Method for Cultivating Samatha and Vipashyana through Seated Meditation; the Essential Heart of the Beginning and End, composed by the Venerable Master Jingxi. As for the Three Truths, they are the innate, natural virtue of one's nature.
The Middle Truth subsumes all phenomena;
the Ultimate Truth dissolves all phenomena;
the Conventional Truth establishes all phenomena.
To raise one is to manifest all three; they are not sequential.
They are inherently possessed by all living beings and are not obtained through artificial effort.

Alas! That the secret treasury remains unmanifested is because it is shrouded by the three delusions: ignorance obscures the *dharmatā*, the dust-like afflictions obstruct the transformative guidance, and the views and thoughts hinder emptiness and stillness.
However, these three delusions are but false imaginings upon the essence itself.
Thereupon, the Greatly Awakened Compassionate Honored One sighed deeply and said:

"Within the realm of True Suchness, the provisional names of 'sentient beings' and 'Buddhas' are utterly absent; within the wisdom of equality, the forms and characteristics of 'self' and 'other' do not exist."
"However, because sentient beings do not realize it through their own direct experience due to their deluded thoughts, they are unable to turn back [from these attachments].
From this, one establishes the three contemplations, shatters the three delusions, realizes the three wisdoms, and accomplishes the three virtues.
The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) destroys the delusions of views and thoughts, realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).

The contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*) destroys the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, realizes the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and accomplishes the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
The Madhyamika practitioner destroys the delusions of ignorance, realizes the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and accomplishes the virtues of the Dharma-body.

However, these three delusions, three contemplations, three wisdoms, and three virtues are not separate entities, nor do they occur at different times; for the principle of naturalness inherently contains all phenomena.
However, the nature of these three truths is thus from the beginning; through delusion regarding these three truths, they are transformed into the three afflictions.

The destruction of these afflictions relies upon the three contemplations; the perfection of these contemplations realizes the three wisdoms; and the perfection of these wisdoms accomplishes the three virtues. From cause to fruit, this is not a process of gradual cultivation.
The sequence of this exposition follows a logical order, though the underlying principle is not sequential.
Such is the general framework; from it, the specific details may be sought.

Regarding the *Record of the Essential Methods for Stopping and Contemplation in Seated Meditation*: Lord Chen Gongguang (Zhongshu Gong) of the Song Dynasty, whose courtesy name was Yingzhong, held that since the mind is fundamentally unmoving, what need is there for "stopping" (*śamatha*)?
Originally, it is not obscured; what need is there for contemplation?
Sentient beings are deluded and distracted, far removed from their original state; they lose both movement and stillness, such that when not in a state of dullness, they are scattered.

These two maladies are the root from which all suffering arises. To cause them to leave suffering and attain peace and security, one should employ *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) as the medicine.
When the illness has been cured, the medicine is discarded and the physician no longer remains; thus, "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) are merely provisional designations.
Being both provisional and empty, they transcend the path of language. Out of great compassion, one speaks without speaking—this is the purpose for which this *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* was composed.
However, its literary expressions and meanings are profound, vast, and boundless, like the great ocean—whom could reach its limits?

Out of great compassion, he further employs skillful means so that by tasting a single drop one may know the flavor of a hundred rivers, and by seeing a single bubble one may perceive the entire body of the tide.
Therefore, outside of the Great Sūtras, this book has also been composed.
Its language is concise and its purport essential, making it easy to understand upon reading; the medicine to cure all ailments is entirely contained herein.

One who skillfully employs medicine does not treat a disease that has already manifested; they halt it before it has dispersed and observe it before it has become obscured. While halting and observing, the condition never becomes obscured and never disperses.
Like the two wings of a bird, like the two wheels of a chariot, there is nowhere far or high that one cannot reach; yet even in arriving at such heights, one does not depart from this. Alas!
If you do not know this, then let it be; but if you know that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* can lead one into the Way, how could you fail to exert yourself?

This "General Outline of Tiantai *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*" was composed by Liang Su, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Acting Right Assistant for Deficiency, of Anding. As for what *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are: they are the means by which one enters the Way.
It guides the principles of all phenomena and returns them to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
What is this limit of reality?
It is the fundamental nature.
The reason why things cannot return to their original state is that obscurity and movement cause it to be so.
To illuminate obscurity is called clarity; to arrest movement is called stillness.
Clarity and stillness are the essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
In the causal stage, these are called *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight);

in the resultant stage, they are called wisdom (*jñāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The causal stage is termed "practice" (*caryā*), while the resultant stage is termed "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
One who practices this is a practitioner; one who realizes this is an achiever.
Originally, the Sage perceived that delusion was sufficient to cause the loss of one's will and movement was sufficient to cause the loss of one's direction;
thereupon he ceased to act and observed, remaining still and clarifying his insight.
It enables movement to be capable of stillness, and stillness to be capable of clarity.
By relying on mutual dependence to establish phenomena, one immediately transcends dependence to illuminate the source.

One sets up the great chariot to guide with rectitude and mounts upon the great task to exercise sovereign power; one attunes the breath of existence within the field of non-duality and inspires the spirit within the realm of the three teachings.
Reaching the most subtle to exhaust one's nature, and reaching the most profound to embody the spirit:
if we speak of what is near, even a single hair’s worth of goodness can lead us through; if we speak of what is far, the gate of the double mystery can be glimpsed.
By employing ultimate perfection to perfect things, nothing is partial;
by employing ultimate reality to realize things, nothing is false.
The Sage sets forth these words to provide demonstration and expands these categories to provide instruction.
To refine them with excellence and soften them so that they seek it for themselves;
to provide models and deliberations so that they arrive at it for themselves—this is the reason for the composition of the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation).
Now, what are the Three Truths?
This is what is meant by "the One.
What are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle?
They are the designations for the One.
"Emptiness and the provisional" are terms for their mutual opposition; "the Middle Way" is a name for attaining oneness.
These are explanations based on discursive thought and do not represent the ultimate principle of oneness.
Ultimate oneness is precisely the three, and ultimate three is precisely the one; it is not so because they contain one another, nor is it so because they produce one another.
This is not a matter of numerical reckoning, nor is it a forced designation; it is the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*). To speak of it and transmit it constitutes its "traces" (*ji*).
The principle is called the root, while the traces are called the branches.
The "root" is the ground reached by the sages;
the "branch" is the teaching manifested by the sages.

Proceeding from the root to manifest its traces, there arise the categories of small and great, universal and particular, sudden and gradual, explicit and esoteric, provisional and real, and fixed and unfixed.
By following these traces to return to the source, one realizes that which is singular and great, perfect and substantial, non-abiding and central, wondrous and the ultimate truth.
These three are the aggregates of the One.
That which is called "emptiness" is spoken of in reference to that which permeates all phenomena;
that which is called "provisionality" is spoken of in reference to that which establishes all phenomena.
The Middle Way is that which articulates the wondrous nature of all phenomena.

In dispelling all delusions, nothing is more effective than emptiness; in establishing all phenomena, nothing is more effective than the provisional; and in ultimately realizing all natures, nothing is greater than the Middle.

If one takes up the "Middle," there is no dharma that is not the Middle; if one regards things as "provisional," what dharma is not provisional? If one takes up "Emptiness," there is no dharma that is not empty.

To perfect these is called the Three Virtues; to cultivate them is called the Three Contemplations. To summarize their essentials, is this not the Sage’s teaching of fathoming the profound, investigating the subtle, exhausting principle, and perfecting nature?

That which is obscure is made clear; that which is obstructed is made permeable. When there is permeability, there is awakening; when there is awakening, one arrives; when one arrives, there is constancy; when there is constancy, there is completion. When there is clarity, there is illumination;
when there is illumination, there is transformation; when there is transformation, there is fulfillment; when there is fulfillment, there is unity.

The Sage has a means by which he encompasses all phenomena without error, pervades all kalpas without omission, sustains as many worlds as grains of sand in the Ganges without attachment, and returns to the state of non-existence without ceasing to exist; we provisionally name him "Buddha" and arbitrarily designate him "Awakened."
To investigate its essential meaning: is there any liberation, mastery, or virtue more supreme and wondrous than this!
Such is the accomplishment of the three contemplations.
What is called "sudden and perfect" (yuantun) is neither gradual nor indeterminate; it refers to the meaning of the ten chapters of the treatise.
The seven chapters are the expansive exposition of the beginning and end, serving as the gateway to the Way.
The five summaries are the elevation of the grand framework, acting as the ferry for crossing the stream.
The ten objects of contemplation are the mechanisms that trigger practice and the truths upon which the meditative observations are established.
The ten vehicles are the gateway for initiating practice, cultivated through sublime function.
That they culminate in right contemplation and conclude with the vision of the realm is because their meaning is complete therein.
To omit the remainder is not the essence of cultivation.
What is it that "mounts"?
It is that which carries all things and sets them in motion.
What are these ten?
They concern the matters of accomplishment and sustenance.
To know the subtlety of the realm and arrive there without traveling is the pinnacle of virtue.
One simply rides upon the One; why rely on the Nine?
These Nine are nothing other than doctrines of mutual production, which are the path trodden by those who have not yet reached the ultimate.
Therefore, one who arouses the mind does so with nothing to be aroused;
one who settles the mind does so with nothing to be settled;
one who shatters all things does so with nothing to be shattered.
As for the other vehicles, he taught them all out of necessity.

When it comes to distinguishing their doctrinal principles, categorizing them into chapters and headings, expanding upon them without becoming prolix, and synthesizing them without being too concise, it is like linked rings that cannot be untied, like strung pearls that cannot be confused, like suspended mirrors that cannot be obscured, and like flowing rivers that cannot be dammed.
The various schools of meaning are many, yet this is not mere contentious debate;
verifying the meanings according to the scriptures is not empty talk;
and distinguishing the shallowness and depth of the four teachings has its source in actual fact.
The causal conditions for accomplishing a single matter are, in principle, left nothing out.
Alas! Is not the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) a treatise that saves the world and clarifies the Way?
Were it not for one whose sage wisdom is transcendent and peerless, standing alone and eminent, who could have accomplished this?
Were it not for one whose intelligence is profound and penetrating, who grasps the spirit while forgetting the form, who could have known this?
People today, however, exclusively rely on the literal words and phrases of the commentaries to interpret them; how can this not be negligent and superficial!
Some even claim:

"The inconceivable realm and the inconceivable phenomena both belong to the domain of the ultimate sages, such that even the Perfected Persons at the stage of Equal Enlightenment have not yet fully exhausted them."

If an ordinary person, whose mind is subject to arising and ceasing and who abounds in the three delusions, seeks to infer the supreme and subtle principle from within the realm of verbal expression, it is like a vinegar gnat attempting to speak of the Great Peng, or a summer insect debating layered ice; that they cannot perceive the truth is self-evident.
The current expositions on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, with their myriad characters and extensive discourses on the stage of fruition, offer no benefit to beginners.
How could they compare to practicing in quietude until one’s own merit reaches its natural culmination? Why must one make premature planning one's primary concern?
This is not so. Regarding the realm of the supreme sages, how could it be separated by vast distances or utterly severed from the ordinary world?
It is simply the single nature; to attain it is awakening, and to lose it is delusion.
It is simply a single principle: through delusion one becomes an ordinary person, and through awakening one becomes a sage.
The deluded person isolates themselves, but the principle is not isolated;
the one who has lost [the way] loses it for themselves, but their nature is not lost.

The composition of the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) is intended to transcend differences and similarities to investigate the sagely spirit, thereby enabling all sentient beings to align their true nature with the fundamental principle.
Aligning one's true nature with the fundamental principle is the means by which one traverses the path of awakening to reach the wondrous realm.
If one does not understand this teaching, then into what shall one's learning enter?
Where shall one's merit be applied?
And from what shall wisdom be aroused?
It is like being without eyes, obscured by the light of the sun and moon, yet traveling through a place of profound peril; to stumble, fall, and be cast down—how could one ever endure it! Alas!
Since the Sage departed long ago and no sages have appeared, those of mediocre and ignorant disposition possess only consciousness.
This has allowed demonic and heterodox delusions to flourish, with various factions burning fiercely together.
There are various claims regarding emptiness: some are submerged in it, while others pierce through it.
Some are stuck to the literal words and dare not move; others drift upon the waves and cannot settle.
Furthermore, there are those who feel content to remain at too great a distance and fail to arrive, and those who perceive that which is too near as being their very own bodies.
There are those who are like withered trees yet claim to have attained meditative concentration; there are those whose hollows resound with cries yet claim to possess wisdom.
There are those who run about in ways that are not the Way yet speak of "expedient means"; there are those who rely on ghosts and spirits yet claim to have spiritual penetration.
There are those who let their minds wander yet claim to be "broad-minded"; there are those who rarely speak yet claim to be "mysterious."
There are those who secretly transmit teachings from tooth to tongue as oral instructions (*mukha-dharma*).
All such individuals establish themselves as patriarchs and their descendants as lineages; they subvert the scriptures and disparage the sages, yet the ignorant remain unaware of it.
Zhongni had a saying:
"I know why the Way is not clearly understood;
it is because of being encumbered by things."
How tragic!
From the year eighteen of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when the Great Master Zhiyi passed away, until the Jianzhong era of our present dynasty, nearly two hundred years have elapsed.

During this time, the transmission of these texts has been maintained by five successive masters: the first was Guanding; the second, Jin Yunwei; the third, Xiaowei of Dongyang; the fourth, Master Lang of Zuoxi; and the fifth, Master Ran of Jingxi.

Among his fellow disciples, Dingtong was foremost in wisdom and understanding; he was able to follow his teacher’s instructions to compile this book because he did not prioritize literary elegance. Consequently, at times it is overly verbose, and at other times it is crude.
During the period between the two Emperors [Gaozong and Zhongzong], it was merely transmitted in sealed secrecy, and its Way did not circulate.
It was only during the Tianbao era that Zuoxi first propagated and explained it, yet those who understood it were but few.
Jingxi extensively compiled biographical records totaling hundreds of thousands of words, encompassing the remnants of the Dharma with such diligence and thoroughness.
Yet after Jingxi’s passing, there were only three or four people who truly understood his teachings.
The ancients said:
"Those who know by birth are the highest; those who know through learning are next; and those who learn because of distress are the lowest.
Now, those who know by birth are surely those whose nature possesses virtue.
Those who learn and thereby know are those whose celestial mechanism is profound;
if one's sensual desires are deep and their ears and eyes are blocked, they will not know even though they study—this is the lowest grade.

Now, as for those who study, they are internally afflicted by obscurations and externally enslaved by distractions; thus, throughout their lives they cannot master the texts, and after several years they cannot obtain any benefit.
Thus, the frequent revisions of the textual phrasing were like shackling one's feet;
the entanglement of sentences was like winnowing chaff that blinds the eyes.
Because teachers were unable to provide clear expositions and disciples were unable to grasp the teachings, it is for this reason that the *Zhi guan* has not yet been fully illuminated in the world.

I have often felt deeply distressed by this state of affairs; therefore, I have straightened its grand framework and grasped its essential points. Wherever principles were obscured or where the teachings were neglected, I have either rearranged them or expanded upon them.
Wherever the meanings were circuitous or the language was vulgar, I have either excised them or polished them.
Generally speaking, of the ten instances of superficiality and negligence, nine have been cured; of the three requirements for breadth and conciseness, only one has been preserved.
This is intended to dispel vulgar stagnation and guide the ignorant youth; as for bequeathing this to others, how could I dare?
If we share the same views and conduct, and do not judge me by the standards of śamatha and vipaśyanā, there will be no concealment between us.
I began this work on the first day of the first month of the Jiazi year of the Jianzhong era, and completed the editing after three years.
When the year reached the ford of Ximu, the work was completed; this is all there is to say.
